proposal: The Mandate says a conservative administration should state that no new direct lending programs will be developed at the SBA and should aim for an end to SBA direct lending. It also recommends working with Congress to assess whether disaster loans should be offered by another agency rather than the SBA and exploring private-sector channels, citing overlap with FEMA aid, weaker incentives to buy insurance, and the fact that more than 90 percent of disaster loans go to individuals rather than businesses.

status_summary: No action ending SBA direct lending, stating that SBA will develop no new direct lending programs, or moving disaster lending to another agency or private channel was found as of 2026-10-18. SBA continues to run and adjust its direct disaster loan program: its disaster recovery official told a House committee on 2025-12-16 that SBA had approved 27,996 disaster loans totaling about $4.76 billion since 2025-01-20 and was moving the lending function into the Office of Disaster Recovery and Resilience, an interim final rule of 2026-01-29 (91 FR 3813) preempts state and local permit delays over 60 days for loan-financed work, and SBA's disaster page (last modified 2026-10-01) lists loans for Hawaii, Alaska and California disasters. The House passed H.R. 4238 on 2026-06-23, which adds reporting and oversight requirements to the disaster loan program without ending or transferring it, and GAO reported on 2026-05-18 that the program made more than 27,000 direct loans in FY2024. The FY2027 SBA request (per CRS, 2026-05-27) would cut disaster loan program funding to $143 million from $282 million, and the FEMA Review Council's final report, approved 2026-05-07, is not described by CRS as addressing SBA disaster loans.

timeline.event: A presidential document on California water and disaster response directs the SBA Administrator, with other officials, to support recovery for North Carolina families, showing a continued SBA disaster role.

SBA's Associate Administrator for the Office of Disaster Recovery and Resilience testifies to the House Committee on Small Business that since 2025-01-20 SBA has approved 27,996 disaster loans totaling about $4.76 billion (64 percent more than the same period of 2024), cut average approval time to 15.4 days, and is moving the disaster lending function back into his office. The testimony does not mention moving the program to another agency or to private lenders (SBA's own figures, not independently checked).
timeline.source: House Committee on Small Business (testimony as posted by the committee's Democratic staff)

timeline.event: SBA publishes an interim final rule, 'Improving SBA Disaster Loan Ability To Provide Meaningful and Timely Assistance' (91 FR 3813), adding 13 CFR part 123 subpart I to preempt state and local requirements that cause permit delays of more than 60 days in work financed by SBA disaster loans; effective the same day, comments due 2026-03-02. SBA cites slow disbursement after the January 2025 California wildfires. The rule does not address who delivers the loans.

The FEMA Review Council approves its final report; a CRS summary (2026-05-15) lists recommendations including up-front formula grants to states for Public Assistance, a single payment for survivors with uninhabitable homes, and moving flood insurance toward private insurers, with no mention of SBA disaster loans, direct loans or private lending.

GAO report GAO-26-108688 on the SBA disaster loan program (about $1.7 billion in lending and more than 27,000 direct disaster loans in FY2024) recommends consistent outreach to survivors; SBA neither agreed nor disagreed. It does not discuss moving the program.

CRS summarizes the administration's FY2027 SBA request: $329.0 million in new discretionary funding (down 74.7 percent), disaster loan program funding of $143.0 million versus $282.0 million in FY2026, zero for nearly all entrepreneurial development programs, and a proposed lender fee in the 7(a), 504 and SBIC programs to offset administrative costs; no proposal to end, transfer or privatize direct or disaster lending is described.

title: End SBA direct lending and explore moving disaster loans to other agencies or lenders
uncertainties: Checked systematically on 2026-10-18. (1) Federal Register API: the researcher's SBA-filtered query on direct lending returned no documents, and a reviewer rerun on disaster loan with transfer and privatize returned SBA size standard proposed rules and a FEMA data-matching notice, which show SBA still administering disaster loans; no document ends direct lending or moves disaster loans. (2) Unified Agenda: item listings could not be reached and the Federal Register fallback was used. (3) congress.gov and govinfo: H.R. 4238, passed by the House on 2026-06-23 and on the Senate calendar since 2026-06-24, and its Senate counterpart S. 300, on the Senate calendar since 2025-03-04, add reporting, budget disclosure and oversight requirements to the SBA disaster loan program and do not end or transfer it; no bill moving disaster lending was found, and bill texts were read only through their CRS summaries. (4) Agency pages: the SBA disaster page (modified 2026-10-01) shows SBA offering loans for several declared disasters; the SBA newsroom could not be loaded. (5) News: one search returned GAO, CRS and older funding items. The FEMA Review Council report and the SBA FY2027 budget justification were not read directly; the first is known from a CRS summary and two press summaries that do not mention SBA, and the second from a CRS Insight, so a recommendation or budget line on SBA disaster loans could sit in the full documents. CRS did not explain the proposed FY2027 cut to disaster loan funding. The testimony figures are SBA's own. Judgment: SBA is continuing and speeding up direct disaster lending, which a reader could classify as diverged from the goal of ending direct lending; not_started is kept because no step toward, or explicit reversal of, the recommendation was found and the FY2027 request halves the program's funding.
